records.title: WASM plan: W9 kept (E-94)
records.text: `wasm/gpuPack.c` (1 298 B) packs pre-render's sprite and caster rows, bit-identical, on the render-queue memory (`f7ad9411`: both queues and both GPU queues as regions of one shared Memory, offsets beside each payload buffer). Kernel, 16k Predator rows on the memory: 3.1× sprites and casters (Node), 2.33× and 2.9–3.0× (a Chrome worker). **painterSort pair (4 pairs): pre-render 44.446 → 42.561 ms, −3.5 %, worse 0/4, KEPT (product).** The profile shows why it is not more: `pack_sprites` still 33.6 % of the saturated worker, against 38.9 % for the JS pack: at 300 000 rows the painter-order gather over a 14 MB queue is the cost. Next: a scatter variant (read in queue order, write to the painter slot), then the Predator gate (pre-render packs its sun casters).

records.title: Instanced-row pack in WASM, E-94 / E-76 W9
records.text: **kept (product).** `wasm/gpuPack.c` packs sprite rows (15 floats) and caster rows (22) as `packInstancedRows` does on its fast paths (world space, no snap, no type filter), with JS's arithmetic, bit-identical (`gpuPackWasm.test.js`). The render queues and GPU queues live in one shared `WebAssembly.Memory` (`f7ad9411`) so the kernel reads the rows where pre-render wrote them; pre-render's `_packRows` takes the kernel and falls back to JS for anything else (Pixi-side packs, the cookie queue, screen space). Kernel (16k Predator rows, both variants on the memory): sprites **3.1×**, casters **3.1×** (Node); a Chrome worker: 2.33× and 2.9–3.0×. Lockstep visual suite: every pixel-compared scene identical. `painterSortStressScene` pair (Chrome, headed, source, 4 pairs, detailed stats off, 300 000 rows): pre-render **44.446 → 42.561 ms, −3.5 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/1 %. Smaller than the pack's 38.9 % share predicts: the CPU profile puts `pack_sprites` at 33.6 % (3 753 ms against `packInstancedRows`' 4 404 in the same window), so at 300 000 rows the pack is bound by its gather in painter order across a 14 MB queue, not by arithmetic. Next: a scatter form (rows read in queue order, written to their painter slot), and the Predator gate (pre-render packs Predator's 13 000 casters). Report: [`reports/E-94-gpu-pack-wasm.md`](./reports/E-94-gpu-pack-wasm.md).

records.title: The pack as a scatter, E-94 W9b
records.text: **kept (product).** At 300 000 rows the WASM pack was bound by its painter-order gather (18 columns read in an order that jumps across a 14 MB queue). `pack_sprites_scatter` / `pack_casters_scatter` build the inverse of the index list, then read the queue in order and write each listed row to its slot; a repeated or out-of-range row makes the kernel decline (-1) and the gather packs. The client scatters lists of at least 4 096 rows that cover half the queue. Bit-identical (`gpuPackScatter.test.js`, which also checks that the scatter ran). An isolated Chrome worker showed only 1.17× over the gather at 300 000 rows on a warm queue; in the scene the queue is cold. **`painterSortStressScene` pair (4 pairs): pre-render 42.474 → 34.324 ms, −18.3 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/2 %; with W9, 44.446 → 34.3 ms. Renderer 2.64 → 2.92 ms, under the floor. Next: the same order in Pixi's pack (Predator packs there).

records.title: Pixi's pack as a scatter, E-94 W9c
records.text: **rejected (regression), reverted.** The W9b order in Pixi's JS pack (`packInstancedRows`' sprite path; Predator packs its sprites in Pixi): an inverse of the painter list, the queue read in order, rows written to their slots, for lists of ≥ 4 096 rows over half the queue. Bit-identical (a test against the kernel's gather). Predator pair (4 pairs, renderer owner): renderer **3.491 → 3.769 ms, +6.4 %, worse 3/4**, cv 2/6 %. At 13 400 rows the queue (650 KB) stays in cache, so the inverse's two extra passes and the scattered writes cost more than the gather's misses; W9b won on a 14 MB queue. The lockstep run also caught a crash on the way (Pixi builds its pack context in `_beginUpload`, without the field the scatter used). A threshold of tens of thousands of rows might still pay in Pixi; not tried.

records.title: Predator gate, W9 + W9b
records.text: **passed on the second sitting.** `runPredatorAbab --vs 5f170e34 --owner preRender`, 4 pairs: the first flagged **physics +3.6 %, worse 3/4** (cv 5/2 %), a worker the pack cannot reach, with pre-render −1.7 % and the rest within 1 %. The rule, set before the second sitting: physics ≥ +3 % at 3 of 4 worse again and the scatter at Predator's size is suspect. The second: physics **−7.9 %** (2/4), pre-render −2.1 %, spatial −4.6 %, renderer −5.9 %, NEUTRAL. Predator's physics moved −9.3 % to +6.7 % across today's gates with no change reaching it: the first flag was drift.

records.title: The visibility sweep without heap numbers, E-95
records.text: **kept (product).** `visPolyStressScene`'s pre-render allocated 37 MB/s in the per-light sweep (`buildVisibilityPolygon` 19.8, `emitVertex` 12.0, `distSqToConvex` 2.6 MB/s). Four causes, found by bisecting a copy of the module under `heapSampleNode.mjs`: (1) doubles passed between functions too big to inline (the sample direction into `emitVertex`, an arc's angles into `emitArcVertices`) and returned (`rayCircleDist`, `rayPolyDist`, `distSqToConvex`): now in a module `Float64Array`, the light still passed through; (2) `let minDist = maxRadius` in `emitVertex`: the parameter had not been used as a number yet, so the loop's merge was typed any value and every closer hit boxed (`+maxRadius` fixes it); (3) `normalizeAngleSigned` at four call sites in a function so big that the inlining budget took one: the angles are normalised in place in two slots by a copy of its arithmetic; (4) `tangentHalfAngle` then fell out of the budget: inlined by hand. Bit-identical: 2 000 random light and occluder sets, 92 282 vertices, every one equal to the old code's. Chrome heap pass, pre-render **37.0 → 2.7 MB/s** (left: `subarray` per light in `buildVisibilityPolygons`, 2.2 MB/s). Pair (4 pairs): pre-render **5.538 → 5.280 ms, −4.1 %, worse 0/4**, cv 2/2 %. W2a (the sweep in WASM) now starts from this JS.

records.title: Instance upload ceiling, E-82 screen
records.text: **the split is worth building.** A temporary hack in `_finishUpload` uploaded 24 of the 68 bytes per pose-interpolated instance (the packing still wrote all 68). `bunnyMarkScene`, 250 000 bunnies, headed Chrome, 2 pairs: renderer **14.040 → 7.595 ms, −44.5 %**, worse 0/2. Pre-render (+118 %) and the main thread (56 → 41 fps) moved with it because the GPU drew the garbage instances (huge stale sprites, overdraw): artifacts of the hack, not costs of a split. About half of Pixi's step at this size is the transfer itself. Next: the per-frame stream (x, y, previous x, y, rotation: 24 bytes) apart from the statics, which are uploaded when pre-render reports a full rewrite.

records.title: The split instance upload, E-82 first sitting
records.text: **regression on presented frames; waits on E-97.** The pose stream (x, y, rotation, previous x, y: 24 bytes) every frame and the statics (44 bytes) per ring slot only when pre-render's new `staticGen` column moves. `bunnyMarkScene`, 4 pairs, renderer owner against `0937669a`: renderer **13.603 → 3.238 ms, −76.4 %, worse 0/4**, but the page **55 → 44 fps** in every pair and pre-render +217 % (cv 30 %). Pre-render's busy time was the same on both sides (CPU trace 603 vs 611 ms/s): its mean had mixed in near-zero backpressure skips, fixed in `0cd085bd`. The frames: with the statics forced up every frame, the split layout presented 54.6 fps, and with a fence check in Pixi 60.0. A fast Pixi oversubscribed a full GPU (E-97). The ceiling screen's pre-render and main-thread moves below were this, not its hack. The gate now judges presented frames (`40bd881d`). Next: the split again on top of E-97.

records.title: Pixi paces its frames to the GPU, E-97
records.text: **kept (product).** A WebGL2 fence after each frame, read two frames later; while it is unsignaled Pixi's tick submits nothing and takes no queue (lockstep always draws, a lost context never waits, eight ticks at most). `bunnyMarkScene` (250 000 bunnies, GPU 3D engine at ~98 % on both sides), headed, 4 pairs, `--owner presented` against `0cd085bd`: presented frames **54.8 → 59.9 fps, +9.1 %, 4/4 higher**, cv 1/0 %. Renderer `STEP_MS` 10.125 → 13.161 ms (+31 %, cv 36 %, not blocking) is the frame mix: HEAD's mean included cheap redraws the compositor dropped, and paced Pixi draws 60 full frames at ~13 ms, about the 803 ms/s HEAD's CPU trace showed. Pre-render 21.682 → 20.970 ms, per worked frame. WebGPU is not paced (E-97b). Report: [`reports/E-97-gpu-frame-pacing.md`](./reports/E-97-gpu-frame-pacing.md).

records.title: The split instance upload on top of E-97, E-82
records.text: **kept (product).** The stashed split, unchanged, against `f59fa284` (E-97 on both sides). `bunnyMarkScene`, headed, 4 pairs, renderer owner: renderer **13.122 → 4.265 ms, −67.7 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/2 %; presented frames 59.9 → 60.0; pre-render 21.110 → 19.084 ms (−9.1 %, worse 0/4: likely less memory traffic beside it, not separated). The split also renders on WebGPU (checked on screen). WebGPU BunnyMark presents **43.2 fps** with Pixi at 2.5 ms: the E-97 symptom, unpaced there (E-97b). Report: [`reports/E-82-split-instance-upload.md`](./reports/E-82-split-instance-upload.md).

records.title: Pixi paces WebGPU frames too, E-97b
records.text: **kept (product); the gate's renderer flag overruled with a CPU trace.** The pacer counts `queue.onSubmittedWorkDone()` completions against submissions (they resolve in order) and waits while the frame before last is unfinished. `bunnyMarkScene?backend=webgpu` (`e55c15a0`), headed, 4 pairs, `--owner presented`: presented frames **43.4 → 60.0 fps, +38.4 %, 4/4 higher**, cv 2/0 %. The gate said REGRESSION on renderer `STEP_MS` 3.311 → 4.277 ms (+29.2 %, 4/4, cv 4/2 %). A CPU trace of each side: Pixi busy 131 ms/s at 41 fps against 175 ms/s at 60, **3.2 → 2.9 ms per presented frame**; pre-render 572 → 794 and logic 98 → 141 ms/s, all running more frames. Unpaced, Pixi's mean mixed upload frames with cheap redraws the compositor dropped. HOW_WE_MEASURE now says how to read this.

records.title: No sprite sort line without Y-sort, E-98a
records.text: **kept (product).** Pre-render computed every collected sprite's sort line (foot Y, a frame lookup when not feet-anchored, the rounded key) although without Y-sort the key is the zIndex alone (`orderSortKey` ignores the Y). It is computed now only where the destination layer Y-sorts; an Adobe root's key still is (its pieces write it). Lockstep visual, balls and oriented: pixels exact. `bunnyMarkScene`, headed, 4 pairs, pre-render owner against `f044d907`: pre-render **18.943 → 12.014 ms, −36.4 %, worse 0/4**, cv 2/1 %; renderer −7.2 %; presented frames 60 both sides.

records.title: Animations advance on persist frames, N-64
records.text: **kept (hygiene).** A bug fix: the persist path skipped the only place sprite animations advanced, so a scene whose rows held still froze them (REVIEW_PLAN N-64). The persist loop reads `isAnimated` per sprite row and runs the clock for animated ones. `bunnyMarkScene` (none animated), 4 pairs against `973f15b9`: pre-render **12.027 → 12.216 ms, +0.9 %** (4/4, cv 1/1 %), renderer +0.4 %, presented 60 both sides.

records.title: No emit loop on a sprites-only persist frame, E-98b
records.text: **kept (product).** On a persist frame whose rows are all sprites, the emit loop only counted the rows (and computed a sort key per row it then skipped); the count is set directly, and the key is computed after the persist skip. Frame moves of animated sprites go to their own count for `staticGen`. `bunnyMarkScene`, 4 pairs, pre-render owner against `1d32263d`: pre-render **12.319 → 11.833 ms, −3.7 %, worse 1/4**, cv 0/3 %; renderer and presented frames unchanged.

records.title: Unmasked sprites straight to the entities collector, E-98c
records.text: **kept (product).** The sprite collect loops called `collectRenderable(0, i)` for every visible sprite: a type dispatch, `Layer.entitiesMask()` and a bit scan that, for a sprite with no layer mask, always end at `_writeRenderable(0, i, Layer.entitiesId)`. The loops now call that directly for unmasked sprites; masked ones keep the generic path (`spriteCollectShortcut.test.js` checks both and that the generic path picks the same collector). `bunnyMarkScene`, 4 pairs against `f8a0ebb6`: pre-render **11.753 → 10.053 ms, −14.2 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/1 %, more than `collectRenderable`'s 13 % self share (likely `_writeRenderable` now inlines with a constant type, not checked). Since E-97: BunnyMark pre-render 21.1 → 10.1 ms per new queue.

records.title: Predator gate, E-97 to E-98c
records.text: **passed (NEUTRAL).** One gate for the batch on shared paths (frame pacing on WebGL and WebGPU, the split pose upload, N-64 and E-98a–c in pre-render's collect and emit): `runPredatorAbab --vs 0cd085bd --owner renderer`, 4 pairs. Pre-render **5.537 → 5.071 ms, −8.9 %, worse 0/4**; renderer −0.5 %, logic −6.3 %, physics −1.3 %, spatial +0.7 % (2/4); presented frames 60 on both sides; load keys within 1 %.

records.title: The body dirty words in 16 bits, E-87
records.text: **kept (product).** `markBodyDirty`'s `Atomics.or` on a 32-bit word with bit 30 or 31 set returned a heap number in Chrome (Atomics run as builtins there): 3.66 MB/s in `spawnStormScene`'s logic worker, and physics' drain `Atomics.exchange` 153 KB/s. Both sides now use a `Uint16Array` over the same bytes (little-endian, so entity i is the same bit as before and the scene's all-dirty fill is unchanged); the drain reads each 32-bit word plainly first and exchanges only the 16-bit halves of a non-empty one. Heap pass after: both 0. `tests/node/bodyDirtyDrain.test.js` runs physics' real drain over words the real marker wrote. `spawnStormScene`, 4 pairs, logic owner against `89aa64d7`: logic **5.302 → 5.184 ms, −4.0 %, worse 0/4**, cv 2/2 %; physics 2.115 → 2.063 ms (below its floor); load keys within 5 %.

records.title: Public `Ray` methods that inline into game code, E-90
records.text: **kept (hygiene).** Game code calling `Ray.cast`, `castAll`, `castDir`, `castWithInfo`, `linecast` or `linecastDir` with doubles boxed each double: the methods (stats `try`/`finally`, setup math) were too big for TurboFan to inline. Each now writes its doubles into `RAY` and calls a body that takes integers and objects, with the stats wrapper in a separate `_xTimed` taken only when `collectDetailedStats` is on. Shrinking those halved the driver's allocation (17.3 → 8.7 MB/s); `hasLineOfSight` and `linecastBetweenEntities`, called in the same function, kept their `try`/`finally`, and inlining budget is per caller: slimmed the same way, the logic worker went **17.6 → 0.29 MB/s** (`rayStressScene?casts=12288`, Chrome heap pass). Pair, 4 pairs, logic owner against `f7d750a6`: logic **9.298 → 9.112 ms, −1.9 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/0 %: a tie on time.

records.title: The visibility polygon copy without views, N-1
records.text: **kept (hygiene).** `buildVisibilityPolygons` copied each light's polygon with `f32.set(outX.subarray(0, n), …)`, two views per light per frame (2.2 MB/s in `visPolyStressScene`, the E-95 heap pass); a loop copies the same Float32 values, clamped to the output length as `subarray` was. Screenshot unchanged. `visPolyStressScene`, 4 pairs, pre-render owner against `f052f897`: pre-render 5.222 → 5.151 ms (−0.3 %, worse 1/4), renderer −0.6 %.

records.title: Poses collected straight into the queue, E-98d
records.text: **kept (product).** The collect stashed each pose (x, y, rotation) and the persist frame copied the stash into the queue's columns. An Adobe root is the only row the emit expands into several, so on a frame without one queue row i is collector row i: the collect writes the poses into the main queue's own columns, and the persist pass (a copied loop) only writes the rotation of sprites drawn with their own facing. With an Adobe root the stash is used as before. Lockstep balls and oriented pixel-exact; the persist test runs both arrangements. `bunnyMarkScene`, 4 pairs, pre-render owner against `63b7dd38`: pre-render **10.100 → 8.665 ms, −14.1 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/0 %. The E-98 series: 21.1 → 8.7 ms per new queue.

records.title: Caster positions in bin order for the shadow stamp, E-99
records.text: **rejected in the kernel.** Predator's CPU profile put 42 % of `stampLightRange` on reading `sun[c * floats]` for each binned caster, so `buildStampGrid` also copied x and y into arrays in bin order and the light walk read those in sequence (bit-identical; `gpuShadowCasters.test.js` passed). `shadowStampMicrobench` (Predator fixture, 48 lights, 16 424 casters), `runKernelsVsRev --vs HEAD`, 5 rounds: stamp **666 → 658 ops/s, −1.2 %**, rounds won 8 %: a tie. The 1.4 MB of caster rows stay in cache; the line's samples were load stalls, not a gather order could fix. Reverted. Busy time in the CPU trace also misled elsewhere this day: Predator's three Box2D pool threads read 1000 ms/s while all of Chrome used 1.9 cores (OS process time), because a thread blocked in `Atomics.wait` samples as busy.

records.title: The decal pixel loop split by blend mode, E-100
records.text: **rejected in the kernel.** `stampToTileBuffers` tested `blendMode === 1` per pixel; two copies of the tile's pixel loop, one per mode, matched the reference (400 stamps, same checksum). `decalMicrobench`, `runKernelsVsRev --vs HEAD`, 5 rounds: primary `normal_multitile_large` 6 731 → 6 710 ops/s (−0.3 %, a tie); `normal_1tile_dense` 0.0 %, `normal_sparse` 0.0 %, `multiply_sparse` −1.9 %, `multiply_1tile_dense` −4.8 %. TurboFan already handled the branch; reverted. The JS loop is near what JS does here: W26 (WASM, SIMD blend) is the remaining lever.

records.title: Decal stamping in WASM, W26 screen
records.text: **scalar port ties JS; parked.** A freestanding C port of `Decal.stampToTileBuffers` for a batch of stamps (64-byte records, tiles at byte 0 of a shared memory, textures beside them, touched tiles listed for the caller to flag; JS-exact ToInt32 and clamped stores) wrote the same bytes as the JS path: 0 of 2 621 440 differing, the same 40 tiles touched (5 000 seeded stamps, dense and sparse textures, both blend modes, 8×5 tiles of 128 px). Node, 9 rounds: JS 49.9 ms, WASM 50.2 ms (×0.99). Plain casts instead of ToInt32 in the pixel loop: 50.3 ms. The loop is bound by its byte traffic and per-pixel branches, which TurboFan compiles as well as clang. Left: SIMD blending with a ±1 tolerance (speed over exactness), or stamping on the GPU into tile render textures (no pixel loop, no upload; changes how saves read tiles). Source kept outside the tree.

records.title: Every light's disc and fan in one draw, E-96
records.text: **kept (product).** Raycasted lighting drew two meshes per light (umbra disc, visibility fan), each with its own uniforms: over 700 draws a frame in `visPolyStressScene`, Pixi's per-draw binding and buffer bookkeeping most of its step. The light's terms are now vertex attributes (40-byte interleaved vertices), every light's disc then fan in light order in one mesh, 32-bit indices, buffers grown to a high-water mark; new GLSL ES 3.00 and WGSL shaders read them as flat varyings. Screenshots at the same moment: 0 of 921 600 pixels differ on WebGL and on WebGPU. 4 pairs, renderer owner against `3995c846`: renderer **5.472 → 1.361 ms, −75.2 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/3 %; presented 60 both sides; Pixi allocation **36.5 → 8.7 MB/s**. Report: [`reports/E-96-light-batch.md`](./reports/E-96-light-batch.md).

records.title: A/A of Predator, the session's noise reference
records.text: `runPredatorAbab --vs HEAD` with the tree at HEAD, 4 pairs: logic −0.9 %, spatial −0.6 %, physics **+3.5 % (worse 3/4, cv 9/2 %, flagged REGRESSION)**, renderer +1.9 %, pre-render +0.3 %. A single 4-pair Predator flag near 3 % is not evidence by itself.

records.title: Pixi's sprite pack through gpuPack.wasm, W9d
records.text: **rejected (logic regression in Predator); code kept outside the tree.** With `packGpuSprites: 'pixi'` and no pose interpolation (Predator), Pixi's entity batch took its rows from new regions of the render-queue memory, and its plain upload went through the W9 kernel on Pixi's own scratch, falling back to JS where the kernel declines; bit-identical against a JS-packed batch, and every Predator pack took the kernel (301 of 301 counted). Predator, renderer owner against `3e2dc99c`, 8 pairs: renderer **3.563 → 3.317 ms, −9.1 %, worse 0/8**, but logic **3.409 → 3.755 ms, +5.9 %, worse 7/8** (cv 7/7 %), which the change cannot reach. Controls the same day: an A/A of Predator (4 pairs: logic −0.9 %, physics +3.5 % at 3/4, so 4-pair flags of that size happen by chance), and W9d's memory layout with the kernel switched off (8 pairs: logic +2.7 %, worse 5/8, NEUTRAL). So logic paid when Pixi got faster (+0.35 ms against Pixi's −0.25 ms), not for the layout; the likely path is a faster Pixi letting pre-render's collect overlap logic's tick on shared cache. Diff and test in scratch, for when the workers' phasing changes.

records.title: The kernels' build-flag pass
records.text: measured, no change. Every shipped kernel (`spatialPublish`, `spatialGather`, `particleIntegrate`, `particleLists`, `gpuPack`) rebuilt with `-mnontrapping-fptoint`: **byte-identical** binaries, because the pinned clang (24.0.0git) already enables it for wasm32. With wasm-opt `-O4` instead of `-O3`: `gpuPack` identical; the other four differ and tie in their own microbenches (Node 22, 5 alternating rounds, one process per run): `spatialGather` +0.5 %, `particleIntegrate` +1.4 % (4/5), `particleLists` −0.6 to +0.7 % across its four cases, `spatialPublish` −0.5 %. `-O3` stays. Not run in Chrome: `-O4` only reorders Binaryen's passes and TurboFan reoptimizes the module; a kernel's own scene sitting is the place to see a difference if one exists. SIMD and float32 per kernel stand as recorded (W8a chose scalar double for correctness, E-18 rejected SIMD for the gather pack).

records.title: The Adobe piece loop with its columns hoisted, E-102
records.text: **rejected (regression), reverted.** `_emitAdobePieces` (36 % of a saturated pre-render in `adobeAnimateScene` at the minimum zoom) read every queue column through `ref` per piece, beside two calls TurboFan left out (`_setQueueType`, `clearTileFields`, the latter 8.2 % self). The 23 columns went into locals before the loop and the two helpers inline; same stores, same values. 4 pairs, pre-render owner, `--camera-zoom min`, against `3c8c7736`: pre-render **26.478 → 27.194 ms, +3.6 %, worse 4/4**, cv 2/2 %. Twenty-three more live values in a function this size most likely spilled registers inside the loop; the reloads were cheaper. Same lesson as review R8: measure a hot-loop restructuring, do not assume it.

records.title: Tile columns cleared only once something tiled, E-102b
records.text: **kept (product).** Every Adobe piece row, every non-sprite row and every plain sprite row wrote zeros into the queue's repeat and tile columns (`clearTileFields`, 8.2 % self of the saturated pre-render in `adobeAnimateScene`). A queue's columns start at zero and only the repeating-sprite branch writes anything else, so the emit keeps the set of tileMode columns that branch has written (per queue buffer and custom layer) and skips the zero writes until its column is in it. Lockstep balls and oriented pixel-exact; a test reuses a repeating sprite's row for a plain one. 4 pairs, pre-render owner, `--camera-zoom min`, against `3c8c7736`: pre-render **26.066 → 23.613 ms, −10.2 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/2 %; renderer +5.4 % at 2/4, cv 25 % (noise). Touches Predator's full emit: for the next Predator gate.

records.title: The painter sorts runs of equal keys as one, E-103
records.text: **kept (product).** An Adobe Animate character writes its pieces into consecutive queue slots under one sort key, and the full painter radix sorted every piece (`radixSortIndicesBySortKey` 17.5 % + `radixPainterOrder` 4.5 % of the saturated pre-render in `adobeAnimateScene`). `radixPainterOrder` now finds maximal runs (consecutive slots, the same key bits), sorts the runs' first slots with the same stable radix and expands each run in place: a stable sort of every row keeps a run together at its first row's place among equal keys, so the order is identical (`painterRunSort.test.js` against the plain radix: dense, filtered with gaps, ties across runs, no runs). When runs do not halve the rows (checked after 1 024 rows) it sorts the rows as before. `painterRadixMicrobench` against HEAD: new `pieces` case **+287 %**, catalog `mixed` +4.1 % (96 % of rounds), `sprites` +1.7 %. 4 pairs, pre-render owner, `--camera-zoom min`, against `186870f6`: pre-render **23.452 → 21.157 ms, −9.8 %, worse 0/4**, cv 0/2 %; renderer −9.8 % (1/4, cv 12 %).

records.title: `TileMap.getTileId`, E-83
records.text: **answered, no change.** `tilemapStressScene` spends 566 ms/s of logic, 80.3 % self in `getTileId` (Q1b), because its 64 queriers ask 16 500 tiles each per tick: 63 M queries/s. `tileMapMicrobench` (Node, the same call with a layer name) reads **2.5 ns per query**. The scene's share (≈7 ns per query under the CPU profiler, Chrome) is the query count, with the profiler's overhead on a call that small; a game asks thousands of tiles per frame, not millions. No sitting: nothing it could find would change a game's frame.

records.title: Predator gate, E-87 to E-103
records.text: **passed (NEUTRAL).** One gate for the batch on shared paths (the body dirty drain by halves, the slim ray entry points, the visibility copy clamp, the aliased pose columns, the batched light mesh, the tile-column skip and the painter run sort): `runPredatorAbab --name gate-E87-E103 --vs 89aa64d7 --owner preRender`, 4 pairs. Pre-render **5.117 → 4.999 ms, −1.3 %, worse 1/4**, cv 2/4 %; logic +2.7 % (3/4, cv 11/4 %, under 3 %), spatial −0.8 %, physics −3.7 %, renderer −1.6 %; presented frames 60 on both sides; load keys within 0.1 %. Predator draws no Adobe Animate character and no visibility polygon, so E-96, E-102b and E-103 have nothing to win there; the gate shows they cost it nothing.

records.title: Every light's self-lit fills in one draw, E-96b
records.text: **kept (product).** After E-96 the self-lit pass (each occluder's own footprint lit again, with a transmit wedge behind occluders that let light through) still made a render call per light: 46 % of Pixi's busy time, inclusive, mostly Pixi's setup per call. Every light's fills, then its wedges (the order the two per-light meshes drew in), now go into one mesh with the light's terms as vertex attributes (52-byte vertices; a wedge's facing radius `1e30` makes its facing term 1), drawn in the light pass after the fans; sprite-masked occluders still draw a pass per light. Screenshots at the same moment: 0 of 921 600 pixels differ on WebGL and WebGPU, with circles, and with a scratch variant at `block = 0.5` (wedges); the lockstep suite's new `vispoly` and `compoundvis` scenes identical. The engine's `maxOccluderSelfLit` of 512 gives only a few dozen lights a pass, so the scene got `?selfLit=N` (`b51de446`). 4 pairs, `visPolyStressScene?selfLit=65536`, renderer owner against `7fb780bf`: renderer **3.395 → 1.197 ms, −64.9 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/1 %; pre-render −1.0 %; presented 60 both sides. Pixi allocation at the default cap **8.7 → 1.8 MB/s**. Report: [`reports/E-96b-self-lit-batch.md`](./reports/E-96b-self-lit-batch.md).

records.title: The transmit wedge without heap numbers, E-96c
records.text: **kept (hygiene).** After E-96b, `_buildSelfLitBatch` allocated 6.5 MB/s at `?selfLit=65536`: `_emitTransmitWedge` took nine doubles per occluder per light and does not inline into the batch, so each call boxed them, although with `block = 1` (every committed scene) it returns at its first line. The batch now calls it only for `block < 1`. On that path the light and the occluder's pose go through a module `Float64Array` (`WEDGE_IN`) and only the entity crosses the call; `_pushWedge`, the tangent helpers and copies of `writeOrientedBoxVerts` / `writePolygonVerts` (same arithmetic, term for term) read them there. Chrome heap pass, Pixi: **6.8 → 0.32 MB/s** at `block = 1`; with every occluder at `block = 0.5` (`?block=X`, `dad840c4`, the first committed scene with transmit wedges) 8.4 → 3.5 MB/s after the arguments alone, **0.33 MB/s** with the helpers. Screenshots with box and circle wedges: 0 of 921 600 pixels differ. No timing pair: Pixi stays under the 3 ms floor at every load the scene reaches (2.2 ms with 2 100 occluders, where pre-render reaches 16 ms), so a pair would FAIL without deciding; the change only removes work.

records.title: The sprite collect writes its own rows, E-98e
records.text: **kept (product).** After E-98d, BunnyMark's pre-render spent 39 % of its busy time in `_writeRenderable`, called once per sprite by E-98c's shortcut: each call re-read the collector's columns, the pose scratch, the custom-collector table and the counters from `this`. The shortcut's sprites always go to the main collector, so both copies of the collect loop (turned camera and not) now write those rows themselves with the columns taken once before the loop; the count lives in a local, synced around `collectRenderable` (masked sprites) and after the loop. A behavioural test fills the collectors through the loop and through `collectRenderable` for every sprite and compares every column, Y-sort on and off (two mutants of the shortcut fail it). 4 pairs, `bunnyMarkScene`, pre-render owner against `a5292000`: pre-render **8.690 → 7.314 ms, −15.8 %, worse 0/4**, cv 2/1 %; renderer −0.4 %; presented 60 both sides; `VISIBLE_ENTITIES` 250 000 both. Touches every scene's sprite collect: for the next Predator gate.

records.title: Bodiless sprites read their pose in the collect, E-98f
records.text: **kept (product).** After E-98e the collect still called `_displayPose` per sprite (14 % self of BunnyMark's pre-render), whose Transform branch is all a sprite without a body needs. Both collect copies read that branch inline (the Transform columns the loop already holds, rotation as `_displayPose` reads it); a sprite whose body has a published pose still calls `_displayPose`. The parity test gained bodies (one with a dead pose rotation, which `_displayPose` sends to the Transform) and Transform rotations; two mutants fail it. 4 pairs, `bunnyMarkScene`, pre-render owner against `25d0c3da`: pre-render **7.441 → 6.070 ms, −18.4 %, worse 0/4**, cv 1/2 %; renderer +0.7 % (4/4, under 3 %); presented 60 both sides; `VISIBLE_ENTITIES` 250 000 both. For the next Predator gate with E-98e.

records.title: A frame the other buffer moved is repaired, not a full emit, E-98g
records.text: **kept (product).** The queue's two buffers alternate. When one buffer's frame advanced an animated sprite, the other still remembered the old frame, and its persist check missed: in a scene of animated sprites nearly every frame became a full emit (a unit test with two sprites on different periods: 20 persist frames of 60). The check now gives that row the current frame's texture (`_repairPersistFrame`, the full emit's `animStart + frame`; it declines, and the frame misses, when there is no animation entry or the frame is past the animation's end), after the animation-state test so a changed animation still misses; `_advancePersistFrame` keeps the buffer's remembered frame in step; a repair bumps `staticGen`. The test: 58 of 60, each buffer showing the current frame on every tick. `animatedSpriteStressScene` (new, `7ef92576`: 100 000 civilians walking on the spot at different speeds, all in view), 4 pairs, pre-render owner against `7ef92576`: pre-render **8.887 → 7.098 ms, −19.3 %, worse 0/4**, cv 3/5 %; renderer below its floor; presented 60 both sides; `VISIBLE_ENTITIES` 100 000 both. For the next Predator gate with E-98e/f.

records.title: Predator gate, E-98e to E-98g and the isolation commits
records.text: **passed on the A/A (NEUTRAL).** `runPredatorAbab --name gate-E98e-g --vs a5292000 --owner preRender`. Four pairs said REGRESSION with every worker worse (pre-render +7.1 %, physics +14.3 %, spatial +4.0 %, renderer +3.3 %, cv 10–19 % on the baseline) while two read-only helper agents ran on the machine; four more pairs on an idle machine (`--append`): pre-render **5.662 → 5.766 ms, −0.3 % paired, worse 4/8**, spatial +6.8 % (6/8), physics +2.9 % (6/8), renderer +1.8 % (5/8), logic +0.9 %, load keys within 0.2 %. Spatial is a worker no commit in the batch reaches. An A/A against the same commit right after (`AA-predator-1023b`, `--vs d3060a97`, 4 pairs) moved every worker one way: pre-render **−5.0 %, worse 0/4** (a "keep" by the rule), logic −7.4 %, renderer −3.9 %, spatial −3.2 % (0/4), physics −2.7 %. On this machine tonight a four-pair Predator verdict cannot see 5 %, and spatial's +6.8 % is inside that: no regression. The kept changes stand on their own scene pairs.

records.title: The spatial row rebuild in C, W6 screen
records.text: **screened (ceiling): +10.9 % in its kernel, about 1.4 % of Predator spatial.** `wasm/test/spatialRebuild.c` is `rebuildOwnedRows` with `getColliderBounds` and `getCellRange` inlined, every shape path, the JS arithmetic in double. `spatialRebuildWasmMicrobench` moves every column the rebuild reads into the spatial publish memory (as Box2D's memory would hold them, Phase 4), so both sides read the same bytes; same checksum over 45 frames of cells, poses and owned lists on Predator's mix and on a mix of every shape. `runKernelVariants`, 5 alternating rounds, Predator's mix (16 500 circles, one worker): JS **2 715 → 3 011 ops/s, +10.9 %**. On the every-shape mix the C is 1.48× (0.85 → 0.58 ms): the JS pays for the non-circle bounds call, not for the loop. The rebuild is 12.5 % of Predator spatial and its JS is close to the floor of its scattered cell writes, so W6 is worth about 1.4 % there; W7 is left with the glue (8 %), and spatial stops being the first reason for the Phase 4 move. Spatial's garbage in Predator, sampled the same day: 17.8 KB/s, nothing to take.

records.title: FSM time in whole milliseconds, E-105
records.text: **kept** (`6b2ed599`). `FSM.tick` passed `FSMClass.time[i]` (a fractional Float32 read) to the state's `onUpdate`, a call TurboFan does not inline (one `onUpdate` per state class): a heap number per tick. The sampling profiler charged it to the game tick that inlined `FSM.tick` (`civilian.js:76` 1 663 KB/s, `person.js:179` 837, `mySoldier.js:60` 347, `fsm.js:136` 340–350). The time now crosses as `time | 0`, whole ms; the column keeps its fractions, and the doc and the type say whole ms. Predator logic garbage with E-104: **2 848 / 2 672 → 212 / 272 KB/s per worker, −92 %** (heapSampleWorkers, 6 s each). Predator, logic owner against `74f41130` (before both), 4 pairs: logic **4.458 → 4.307 ms, −1.9 % paired, worse 2/4** (cv 12/2 %), no worker 3 % worse (spatial +2.6 %, pre-render +1.6 %), load keys within 0.1 %: NEUTRAL, which tonight's A/A says a four-pair Predator verdict cannot resolve below 5 %. E-68 (2026-10-21) screened this as a public signature change for ~0.5 %, from 0.8 MB/s: the signature stays, the value is whole ms, and the sites inlined into game ticks had not been counted.

records.title: Query type masks as index lists, E-104
records.text: **kept (hygiene)** (`564fccc4`). `copyActiveMatchesToBuffer`, `query()` and `_buildQueryResult` walked each type mask in BigInt (`countTrailingZeros`, `mask &= mask - 1n`), which allocates per step; publishing the precomputed queries every frame made 199 KB/s in each Predator logic worker. Each mask's type indices are an `Int32Array` built with the query, lowest first (the bit walk's order); the class version's closure per query per publish went too. With E-105, one Predator pair (below). A test walks a sparse 64-type mask (types 0, 5, 33, 63) through `query()`, the slow active path and the publish, and passes on the old code as well.

records.title: The persist check and the pose pass in one walk, E-98h
records.text: **dropped (tie); diff in scratch.** After E-98g BunnyMark's pre-render profile put the persist check at 23 % and the poses-only pass at 17 %, two walks of every row; one walk (`_type0PersistPoses`, −1 on a miss) did both, with the animated rows advanced only after every row passed (a walk that misses on a late row would otherwise advance them twice, once there and once in the full emit; a new test fails a mutant that advances inline). 4 pairs, `bunnyMarkScene`, pre-render owner against `74f41130`: pre-render **6.174 → 6.244 ms, −0.3 % paired, worse 2/4**, renderer +0.4 %. The two walks' shared loads were not the cost; each row's own work is. Reverted; the diff is `E-98h.fused-persist.diff` in the session scratch.

records.title: Where the rest of the garbage is (heap pass over seven scenes after E-104 to E-108)
records.text: in game and bench code, mostly fractional doubles in GameObject instance fields written every tick (`painterMoveStressScene`'s `this._phase +=`: 21 MB/s; `bichosScene` 7 MB/s), which Chrome keeps as tagged fields, a heap number per write; per-entity doubles belong in a component. Engine sites left above 100 KB/s: Pixi's vendored WebGL resource bind (`for…in` over shader groups per draw, 500–700 KB/s in Predator, bichos, littleCity), `_applyContactBegin`'s pair map (75–170 KB/s, W18), `_emscripten_get_now` in the Box2D thread (210–340 KB/s), Pixi `updateLighting` (220–270 KB/s in Predator), `syncParticleFeed` (80–170 KB/s).

records.title: `rng()` without the closure call, E-106
records.text: **no change; reverted.** `littleCityScene`'s logic made 3.4 MB/s in `rng` (from `cityPerson.tick`). `rng()` stepping the seeded state itself (no call to `globalThis.rng`) left it at 4.2 MB/s: the box is where `rng()` returns into a game tick too big to inline it, not inside. A double-returning API stays boxed at an uninlined caller.

records.title: Decal tile premultiply views made once, E-107
records.text: **kept (hygiene)** (`3c806eae`). `copyPremultiplyRgba` made two `Uint32Array` views per tile per upload: Pixi **3 658 → 76 KB/s** in `decalBlitStressScene`. Pixi keeps the views beside its tile buffers. No pair: it removes two allocations and nothing else.

records.title: Decal stamps enqueue through a module array, E-108
records.text: **kept (hygiene)** (`8ad26b2a`). `Decal.stamp` wrote each resolved field into a scratch op object (a tagged field in Chrome) and passed five doubles to `enqueueStamp`: 3.2 MB/s of logic garbage in `decalStampStressScene`. Plain numbers are taken as given; x, y, scale and alpha reach the ring through a `Float64Array`, and `enqueueStamp` keeps its signature. Logic **7 923 → 4 746 KB/s**; the rest is the bench driver's config literals. A test reads back the ring for number, range and default fields, and passes on the old code too. No pair: logic there is the driver.

records.title: The per-entity stamp skips the per-light index sort, E-110
records.text: **kept** (`5b392b7b`). The grid walk sorted each light's candidates by caster index (a typed-array sort with a JS comparator) so its rows match a serial scan. With `maxShadowsPerEntity` each kept caster only takes the light into its own slots and the rows are appended per caster afterwards, so the order inside one light changes nothing; Predator runs 3 per entity and 512 per light. `shadowStampMicrobench` (Predator fixture, 48 lights) **672 → 916 ops/s, +36.4 %**, 5/5 rounds, checksum equal. A tie-free dense test compares the grid walk with the full scan and passes on the old code too. Predator pair, pre-render owner, 4 pairs against `71008fca`: **NEUTRAL**, pre-render +0.9 % paired (2/4 worse, cv 20/12 %), with logic, physics and renderer 4–6 % faster on the same side (drift on a busy machine). The scene did not get 3 % worse, so the kernel claim stands.

records.title: The stamp grid's cell computed once, E-111
records.text: **open: ties by the rounds rule in four kernel sittings; diff in scratch.** `buildStampGrid` bins every caster twice, in its count pass and in its fill pass, each time with `Math.floor((x - minX) / 256) | 0`. Computing the cell once, by an exact multiply with 1/256 (truncation equals floor there, since x − minX ≥ 0), and keeping it in a module `Int32Array` for the fill pass: `shadowStampMicrobench` stamp case **+17.7 %** (72 % of rounds won), **+10.5 %** (73 %), **+16.7 %** (86 %), **+13.5 %** (82 %, 15 rounds), checksums equal in all four. Every sitting is a TIE under the 90 % rule; the machine was loaded each time (a demo tab and the dev server, then VS Code). Rerun on a quiet machine, or let W23's port absorb it. Diff: `D:\tmp\p4\e111.patch`.

records.title: Queue columns a multiple of 4 KB apart alias in cache, E-113 (found in the W4a sitting)
records.text: **open.** The render queue's columns are `capacity × 4` bytes apart (`renderQueueLayout.js`), so at a capacity that is a multiple of 1 024 every float column of a row falls in one L1 set. In the W4a kernel, capacity 32 768 against 33 000 (same rows, same checksum): the JS emit **885 → 988 ops/s (+11 %)**, the C emit **882 → 2 150 (2.4×)**. Predator's capacity (119 298) spreads them; proceduralTree's 8 192 does not, and component columns (`count × 4` apart, element alignment only) do the same at entity totals at or next to a multiple of 1 024 (queryChurn and spawnStorm declare 8 193). Candidate: start each queue column a cache line later than the last (`renderQueueLayout` is the one layout every reader takes), and in `Component.initializeArrays` if a scene shows it (its hand-mirrored layouts in `physicsHostImpl.js` first).

records.title: WASM plan: W4a wired and kept (E-112)
records.text: Components bind at a byte offset (`658bdb54`); with `wasm.preRenderEmit` the render-queue memory is made first and holds the SpriteRenderer, ShadowCaster and DecorationComponent blocks and the emit's state (`4e37b91b`; lockstep visual suite identical); the kernel ships as `src/workers/preRenderEmit.wasm` with its client (`5acea239`) and `emitSpriteQueue` hands it every full emit, writing the listed particle, glow and bullet rows after it in JS (`6dd088e2`). Through the worker, 30 frames with and without the kernel give the same queue byte for byte; all 8 bundles embed and load the module. Chrome: Predator `EMIT_MS` 1.24 → 0.92 ms. **Predator gate, 8 pairs: pre-render 5.054 → 4.666 ms, −4.6 %, worse 2/8, KEPT (product)**; the runner's REGRESSION on spatial (+5.1 %, 6/8) did not reproduce in a same-build pair (+1.0 %), and the session's A/A flagged the renderer at +6.6 % (4/4) on identical code (REVIEW_PLAN M13). Report: [`reports/E-112-preRender-emit-wasm.md`](./reports/E-112-preRender-emit-wasm.md). Next: W23.

records.title: Pre-render's emit in C, E-112 (W4a)
records.text: **kept (product).** `wasm/preRenderEmit.c` (3 021 B, `src/workers/preRenderEmit.wasm`) writes `emitSpriteQueue`'s full-emit rows for sprites and decorations on the render-queue memory: the sort key, the shadow terms, the tile fields and the animation clock in double as the JS does them, `proxyToGlobalAnim` and the frame tables as flat arrays. Rows of other types (particles, glows, bullets, trails) are listed and written after it by a copy of the loop's branches; play-once ends and missing textures come back as lists; Adobe and LiquidFun frames, custom layers and persist frames keep the JS loop. Wiring (`658bdb54`, `4e37b91b`, `5acea239`, `6dd088e2`): components bind at a byte offset, and SpriteRenderer, ShadowCaster and DecorationComponent live in the render-queue memory with the emit's state (lockstep visual suite: every exact scene identical); switch `wasm.preRenderEmit`. Kernel (`f46a8ae3`, Predator's mix at its queue capacity, Node 22): **976.7 → 2 124.5 ops/s, +117.5 %, 25/25**, checksums equal over 45 frames; through `emitSpriteQueue`, 30 frames with and without the kernel are byte for byte the same, other row types included. Chrome, Predator, detailed stats: `EMIT_MS` **1.24 → 0.92 ms (−26 %)**. **Predator gate against `22a9aa87`, 8 pairs, owner pre-render: 5.054 → 4.666 ms, −4.6 %, worse 2/8**; the runner read REGRESSION on spatial +5.1 % (6/8), which a same-build pair (only the kernel call switched off on side A) did not reproduce (+1.0 %) and which this session's A/A matches in size on another worker (row above); logic +0.8 %, physics +1.1 %, renderer −2.3 %, load keys within 0.1 %. Re-measured with the window watched (2026-10-24, the stamp switched off with `wasmOff=shadowStamp`, 4 pairs): **pre-render 5.407 → 5.255 ms, −5.2 %, worse 1/4, KEPT**; spatial +0.8 %. Report: `reports/E-112-preRender-emit-wasm.md`.

records.title: WASM plan: W23 kernel sitting (E-114)
records.text: `wasm/test/shadowStamp.c` (8 658 B, a test module) is `stampLightRange` whole: the stamp grid, each light's gather, the index sort without a per-entity cap, takeClosest's quickselect and quicksort (the same pivots, so the same casters on ties), the per-caster nearest lights and the append. Distances are stored as float where the JS stores them into a Float32Array, and `Math.floor(..) | 0` goes through an exact ToInt32 (V8's DoubleToInt32) for coordinates past 2^31. The lights become a table of five doubles, written by the wrapper on every call. `shadowStampWasmMicrobench` (`bcaba94e`) on the Predator fixture (48 lights, 16 424 casters, 512 per light, 3 per entity), every array in one shared memory: checksums equal over the stamp rows, their light indices and the cursor; **897.7 → 1 794.0 ops/s, +99.8 %, 25/25** (Node 22, 5 alternating rounds); the plain path 810 → 1 839 ops/s. Kernel → scene gate: the stamp's call tree was 32 % of Predator pre-render before E-112, so about 16 % of it. Next: the wiring on the render-queue memory.

records.title: WASM plan: W23 wired and kept (E-114)
records.text: The render-queue memory gets the stamp's regions (`1d8ffe1f`): the candidates, distances, order and kept list, the 128 × 128 grid, the nearest lights per caster and a light table, sized from the GPU queue's sun cap and the lighting config. The kernel ships as `src/render/shadowStamp.wasm` with its client (`688bc147`), which writes the lights and declines a call the regions cannot hold; `_stampAgainstSun` stamps through it (`d66e192d`). Parity: 240 random frames bit for bit, a worker-level check, and two meaningful mutants caught. All 8 bundles embed and load the module. Chrome: Predator `SHADOW_Q_MS` 2.57/2.78 → 1.92/1.96 ms. **Predator gate, window watched, 4 pairs: pre-render 5.287 → 4.692 ms, −10.3 %, worse 0/4, KEPT (product).** The same night the gate's minimized-window problem was found and fixed (REVIEW_PLAN M13). Report: [`reports/E-114-shadow-stamp-wasm.md`](./reports/E-114-shadow-stamp-wasm.md).

records.title: WASM plan: W4a kernel sitting (E-112)
records.text: The re-measured premise is on record: after E-98 the emit and collect chain is 43.6 % of Predator pre-render (`emitSpriteQueue` 17.2, `collectVisibleEntities` 9.6, `_storeEntitySortY` 5.1, `_displayPose` 5.0, `_writeQueueShadow` 4.1, `spriteSortFootY` 2.6 %) and 96 % of BunnyMark's (collect 55.0, persist check 23.0, poses-only 16.4 %). W4 splits: the emit reads no Box2D memory, since the collect writes its poses into the queue columns (E-98d) and the queue is in the render-queue memory (W9), so **W4a** (the emit) can go first on that memory; **W4b** (the collect) reads Transform from Box2D's heap and stays behind Phase 4. `wasm/test/preRenderEmit.c` (2 982 B) against the shipped `emitSpriteQueue` on Predator's mix at its queue capacity (119 298 rows), every column the emit reads in one memory, checksums equal over 45 frames: **976.7 → 2 124.5 ops/s, +117.5 %, 25/25** (Node 22, TurboFan both). Cache-resident (`--scale 0.05`) the C is 2.1× the JS; the JS costs 41–48 ns a row at any size, so it is bound by its instructions and the C by memory. Kernel → scene gate: about 11.5 % of Predator pre-render. Found on the way (E-113): at a capacity that is a multiple of 1 024 the queue's float columns alias in L1; at 32 768 both sides tied (885 and 882 ops/s), at 33 000 the JS read 988 and the C 2 150. Next: wiring (components bound at byte offsets in the render-queue memory; the kernel writes sprite and decoration rows and lists the rest for the JS).

records.title: WASM plan: W9b kept (E-94)
records.text: The scatter form: `pack_sprites_scatter` / `pack_casters_scatter` invert the index list, read the queue in order and write each row to its slot (a repeated or out-of-range row declines to the gather). The client scatters lists of ≥ 4 096 rows over half the queue. Warm, in a Chrome worker, it was only 1.17× the gather at 300 000 rows; on the scene's cold queue: **painterSort pre-render 42.474 → 34.324 ms, −18.3 %, worse 0/4, KEPT (product)**; 44.4 → 34.3 ms with W9. W9c (new): Pixi's JS pack (Predator packs there) gathers in painter order too.

records.title: WASM plan: W25 kept (E-81)
records.text: `spatial.gatherCellOrder` on by default. **Boids pair (6 pairs): spatial 7.462 → 6.942 ms, −8.4 %, worse 0/6, cv 3/3 %, KEPT (product).** Predator, two gates: the first NEUTRAL at cv 12–21 % (the owner's own Chrome was busy); the second flagged spatial +6.6 % (5/6) while every worker the change cannot reach drifted the same way (logic +4.1, physics +5.9, pre-render +3.2, renderer +2.1 %). The sort itself costs 11.4 µs a frame at Predator's batch (one spatial worker, ~1 200 rebuilds a frame; 3.1 µs at 300, 43 µs at 4 600), 0.25 % of its 4.5 ms spatial step, and the kernel with Predator's settings was +2.3 %: the flag is the session's drift, not the order.

records.title: WASM plan: Q1b, every scene profiled
records.text: See [Q1b](#q1b-every-scene-2026-10-23): new rows W24–W28, W9, W11, W14, W19 and W22 widened, the order above.

records.title: WASM plan: W13 kernel sitting (E-80)
records.text: `wasm/particleLists.c` (a candidate): `buildActiveAndVisibleListBuffers` and `…Turned` over the whole pool, and the no-camera list. The active column is read 16 slots at a time (`i8x16`): an empty block is skipped, a full one runs straight through, a partial one visits its live slots in order. Each list is u16 [count, …], and the visible list may hold one index past its count (the index goes in before the test decides); `isItOnScreen` is written for live particles only, as JS writes it. The published active list is the integrate's input, so the worker's local copy goes. Two variants, both bit-identical: scalar (each particle in double) and **f64x2** (a full block's tests two particles per operation on the same doubles, its flags and active indices stored as vectors). `particleListsWasmMicrobench`: the `?tween=1` stress population aged 300 frames by the shipped integrate (65 174 live of 65 535; 3 752 full blocks, 343 partial), four cameras. Same checksum as JS over both lists and every flag. Alternating processes, 5 rounds (Node 22, AC; TurboFan, checked with natives in a single run): | case | JS | scalar | f64x2 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | stress (zoom 0.3, 51 792 visible) | 1 742.9 ops/s | 5 999.0, +244.2 % | **7 469.1, +328.6 %** | | zoomed (zoom 1, 13 822 visible) | 852.1 | 5 990.9, +603.0 % | **7 364.8, +764.3 %** | | turned (zoom 0.6, 0.785 rad) | 3 653.5 | 4 488.3, +22.9 % | **5 859.8, +60.4 %** | | sparse (10 000 slots, 148 live) | 63 366.3 | 639 250.6, +908.8 % | **741 373.4, +1 070.0 %** | f64x2 beats JS 25/25 in every case and the scalar variant 25/25 in the three dense ones (sparse runs the same code in both: 20/25). The JS unturned loop branches on the test, so a camera that sees part of the pool costs it 2× (1.17 ms at 65 k); the turned loop is branchless already. Kernel → scene gate: 22.6 % of the stress scene's particle worker before W12 (Q1), about a third after it; 0.574 → 0.134 ms a call here. Next: wiring, f64x2 only.

records.title: WASM plan: owner question on `fdlibmSincos.h`
records.text: WebAssembly has no sin or cos instruction, and C's `sin` would link this same musl code, whose large reduction needs the stack T6 forbids; a `Math.sin` import would be a second import and a boundary call per particle. Only accuracy was measured (Q2) and the whole kernel (spin +107.9 %), never the trig alone against a cheaper one. Open as a W12 variant under decision 5: a float32 polynomial sincos, timed in the spin case (only rotating particles reach it; the stress mix and Predator do not).

records.title: WASM plan: W12 wired and kept (E-79)
records.text: `createParticleMemory` (memory map `particleIntegrateRegions`) gives ParticleComponent a shared `WebAssembly.Memory` as its buffer. The component sits at byte 0, so every worker's views are unchanged, and the worker's lists and the kernel's scratch follow it. `particleIntegrateClient.js` binds the module, writes the column table and copies `particleTween.js`'s EXPO tables (`expoLutTables`). `integrateParticlesWasm` drains the dead list and the trig list; the particle worker chooses it per frame in `updateParticlePhysics`, behind `wasm.particleIntegrate` (default on). `tests/node/particleIntegrateWasm.test.js` boots a real particle worker per thread, both paths, 40 frames, two mixes: identical state. Bundles: three modules embedded and loading in all 8. **Stress pair (Chrome, `?tween=1`, 6 pairs): particle 4.249 → 2.935 ms, −31.3 %, worse 0/6, KEPT (product)**; pre-render +1.3 % (4/6), `ACTIVE_PARTICLES` within 0.0 %. **Predator gate: NEUTRAL** (particle under the floor at ~100 particles; logic +2.6 % (5/6), physics +2.2 %, spatial +1.4 %, none at 3 %). Report: [`reports/E-79-particle-integrate-wasm.md`](./reports/E-79-particle-integrate-wasm.md).

records.title: WASM plan: W12 kernel sitting (E-79)
records.text: `wasm/particleIntegrate.c` (4 629 bytes; a candidate): the integrate's three passes, with every input widened to double and each store converted as the typed array does (float32 rounding, ToUint16 with its wrap). JS keeps what sits around the loop: the dead list becomes `returnToPool` calls in the order JS made them, which matters because the free list's order decides later allocations. The rare angle past fdlibm's medium reduction goes back to `Math.cos`/`Math.sin`. Rotation uses `wasm/fdlibmSincos.h`: musl's fdlibm code inlined, so the kernel needs no stack; the T6 check confirms it. The EXPO tables are copied from JS's, never recomputed in C. `particleIntegrateWasmMicrobench`: the `?tween=1` stress scene's driver through the shipped `ParticleEmitter.emit` (seeded), 65 535 particles, `ParticleComponent` laid out from byte 0 of a shared `WebAssembly.Memory` with the lists and scratch after it. The state is identical after every one of 60 frames, in both cases. Alternating processes, 5 rounds (Node 22, AC): **tween** 327.9 → 528.1 ops/s, **+61.0 %**, 25/25; **spin** (rotation, angular velocity and tint tweens on every particle) 122.9 → 255.5, +107.9 %, 25/25. Kernel → scene gate: the integrate is 75 % of the stress scene's particle worker (Q1), so about a quarter of it at this speed-up. Next: wiring.

records.title: The Predator gate reads the main folder, E-119's first sitting
records.text: **void; the runner fixed.** A batch gate (W4c to W22 against `1cbc02b1`, particle owner) read every worker worse on B: logic +8.3 % (4/4), physics +12.1 % (4/4), spatial +4.7 %, renderer +3.8 %, pre-render +7.6 % (4/4), against BunnyMark's −15 % for the same pre-render changes. records.title: Three agent kernels screened, E-120 to E-122

W11's author found half its copy is UVs that never change (E-118, open).

records.title: Decoration sway in C, E-119 (W22)
records.text: **kept (kernel; the floor keeps the product from judging it).** `wasm/decorationSway.c` (an agent's screen, `7c6d42c5`) is `_updateDecorationSwayBuckets`' per-decoration loop with its bucket cache and impulse step; the per-bucket Math.sin / Math.cos and every decoration needing its own (an impulse's phase, an angle of 0.08 rad or more) stay JS. Kernel, Predator's 20 000 blades, 10 248 on screen: **5 681.6 → 11 050.9 ops/s (+94.5 %, 25/25)**. Wired: the sway arrays become regions of the render-queue memory next to the decorations block (`0433e6cc`), the module ships with its client (`f86afae5`), the particle worker binds it and finishes the listed decorations (`4bad5d36`); a test boots a worker on such a memory and runs 60 random frames, bit for bit. No scene can judge it on STEP_MS: the sway costs 22 ns a decoration (H-10) and the snapshot is u16, so 65 535 decorations stay near 1.6 ms of particle, under the 3 ms floor. Predator, both sides in worktrees, against `1cbc02b1` with the persist series, 4 pairs: particle 0.942 → 0.870 ms (−7.6 %, under the floor), no worker consistently worse.

records.title: Persist frames without shadow casters, E-117
records.text: **kept (product).** Without ShadowCaster, every sprite row's shadow terms are the zeros the full emit wrote when the buffer last held the row; `EMIT_NO_CASTERS` leaves them (about 3 MB a frame in BunnyMark). Kernel: **594.2 → 782.5 ops/s (+31.7 %, 25/25)**. Wired in `7a06ab3e`; the persist schedule now changes casters with no dirty flag (`e74919fc`), which caught a walk that never wrote them. Gate with E-116, BunnyMark against `f0237dd0`, 4 pairs: **pre-render 5.644 → 5.174 ms, −7.7 %, worse 0/4**, renderer +0.1 %. BunnyMark's pre-render over the series: 6.12 → 5.17 ms.

records.title: The persist check and the poses in one walk, E-116
records.text: **kept (product).** `persist_frame` replaces `persist_check` and `persist_poses`: the pose writes go out as the walk checks each row (a miss's full emit rewrites them), the animation clocks after the walk, in row order (E-98h's JS fusion tied; in C the second walk's reads count). Kernel (`84ad00b3`): **534.1 → 594.2 ops/s (+11.3 %, 25/25)**. Wired in `b8a3af2c`; the tests hold it to the JS with a full emit and the remember after each miss on both sides; three mutants fail them.

records.title: The persist path in C, E-115 (W4c)
records.text: **kept (product).** `persist_check`, `persist_poses` and `persist_remember` in `wasm/preRenderEmit.c` are `_type0PersistHit` (with `_repairPersistFrame`), `_writeType0PosesOnly` (with `_writeQueueShadow` and `_advancePersistFrame`) and `_rememberType0Set`, on the emit table and the remembered rows, now regions of the render-queue memory (`abac8a72`, `00ed7598`); wired in `7a839d29`. Kernel (`1ec43ab7`, BunnyMark's 250 000 sprites): a persist frame **395.8 → 541.1 ops/s (+36.7 %, 25/25)**, a remember **665.8 → 1 530.6 (+129.9 %, 25/25)**; alone, the check 3.1× and the remember 4×, the poses-only pass 1.38 → 1.26 ms (three shadow zeros and two flags a row: memory traffic either way). Gate, BunnyMark against `1cbc02b1`, 4 pairs: **pre-render 6.121 → 5.699 ms, −6.9 %, worse 0/4**; renderer +1.8 % (3/4). Predator, both sides in worktrees, against `1cbc02b1` with W22, 4 pairs: pre-render −3.4 % paired, worse 1/4 (cv 10 %), no worker consistently worse. Report: `reports/E-115-preRender-persist-wasm.md`.

records.title: The flowfield search in C, E-122 (W14)
records.text: **kept (product).** An agent's `wasm/navFlowfield.c` is `computeFlowfield`'s search, walls' pass and smoothing, bit for bit; the nav buffer is now byte 0 of a WebAssembly.Memory with the search's scratch after it (`6fe64c1a`), the module ships with its client (`0995b2cf`) and the particle worker runs it (`0786a06c`). Kernel (`f0237dd0`): **710.0 → 11 369.4 flowfields/s (16×, 25/25)**. Gate, navStress against `54b09f41`, both sides in worktrees, the throughput as the owner (`--owner FLOWFIELDS_COMPUTED`, `54b09f41`, `c9f0377e`): **FLOWFIELDS_COMPUTED 6.1 → 36.8 a frame (+509 %, 4/4)**, every request served inside the 8 ms deadline; particle STEP_MS **8.689 → 3.729 ms (−56.9 %, 0/4 worse)**; every other worker under the floor.

records.title: A/A of Predator on exact windows, the session's noise reference
records.text: The session's noise reference, and the first sitting on exact windows (`34bc7229`, `630526e7`: every frame of the window counted, primary `STEP_MS − WAIT_MS`). `runPredatorAbab --name aa-2026-10-24 --vs 6d9c7258 --hyp-rev 6d9c7258`, Predator, headed, source, detailed stats off, 4 pairs, both sides in worktrees of one commit. **NEUTRAL**: logic 4.771 → 4.626 ms (−1.1 %), spatial 5.549 → 5.472 (+0.9 %), physics 8.206 → 7.857 (−2.1 %), renderer 4.307 → 4.109 (+0.1 %), pre-render 5.837 → 5.508 (−2.3 %), each worse in 2 of 4 pairs; presented 60.0 both sides; load within 0.5 %. The paired deltas move together across workers within a run: pairs 1 and 2 read side B +4 to +11 % on every worker, pairs 3 and 4 −6 to −15 %. So the run-to-run swing is the machine's, shared by all workers, and per-worker detection limits at 4 pairs are wide (2.5 × paired sd / √4): logic 9.7 %, spatial 12.2 %, physics 14.5 %, renderer 14.1 %, pre-render 14.8 %. Read a Predator owner against the workers the change cannot reach in the same runs (HOW_WE_MEASURE's drift rule), not against these limits alone.

records.title: BunnyMark's pre-render after the persist series: the collect is 70 %, E-128 and E-98
records.text: A CPU profile of `bunnyMarkScene` (250 000 sprites, all on screen) after the persist series (E-115 to E-117): `runIntegratedWorkerBenchmark --headed --trace-cpu --src --no-collect-detailed-stats`, summarised from 10 s. Pre-render (239 ms/s busy, GC 0): `collectVisibleEntities` **69.9 % self**, its hot lines the row writes inlined there since E-98e/f (`rY[n] = keyY` 10 %, `cPx[n] = pose[0]` 9 %, `cRotS` 8 %, `rIndex` 8 %, `cPy` 7 %, `rType` 7 % of that self time); the persist kernel (`persist_frame`, W4c) 26.1 %; nothing else over 1 %. Pixi (196 ms/s): `_packPoseOnly` 68 %, `updateBuffer` 13 %. **E-128 answered:** the cull-and-collect loop is far past W3's reopen trigger (18 %), so W3 folds into W4b, the collect in C, whose rows and poses need Transform in the kernel's memory: Phase 4, with the collect as its first mover (the plan named spatial first, but W6 screened at 1.4 %). **E-98 closed:** the question in its title is answered, pre-render's full emit at 250 000 sprites takes 21.1 → 5.17 ms per new queue (E-98a–g, then E-115 to E-117), under a frame; what is left of the worker is the collect, W4b.

records.title: Pixi's sprite pack in C on one build, with the rows copied before the upload, E-123 (W9d)
records.text:
**kept (product).** W9d, Pixi's plain sprite pack through `gpuPack.wasm`, rebased onto the emit, stamp and sway regions behind `wasm.pixiPack` (`6d9c7258`) and timed on one build: `runPredatorAbab --vs <rev> --query-a wasmOff=pixiPack --owner renderer`, side A the JavaScript pack, side B the kernel, one worktree for both (no side bias), exact windows, headed, source, detailed stats off, 4 pairs.

**Owner scene first:** `renderQueueStressScene` (48 000 plain sprites, 18 880 in view) puts the renderer at 1.438 → 1.183 ms (−17.7 %, 4/4), under the 3 ms floor, so it is not judged there; the scene has no load knob yet. Predator's renderer (4–5 ms, Pixi packs its sprites) is the owner instead.

**First Predator sitting** (the batch's rows were the shared rows themselves, so the Pixi buffer uploaded from the WebAssembly.Memory): renderer 4.126 → 3.937 ms, **−5.1 %, worse 0/4**, but every worker the change cannot reach slower on the kernel side in every pair: physics +9.5 % (4/4), spatial +6.3 % (4/4), pre-render +6.1 % (3/4), logic +4.7 % (3/4); verdict REGRESSION. The same shape as W9d's 2026-10-23 sitting (logic +5.9 %, 7/8), now with no second directory to blame. The one thing besides the kernel that set W9d apart from the default path was the upload: `_commitPackedBatch` copies pre-render's rows into a private array first.

**Second sitting, with that copy** (`365c4b60`: the kernel packs into the shared rows, the batch copies them into its own array, the buffer uploads that): renderer 4.864 → 3.980 ms, **−10.6 %, worse 1/4**, cv 12/10 %; logic +2.7 % (2/4), spatial −6.1 %, physics −9.5 %, pre-render −3.9 %; presented 60.0 both; load within 0.1 %. Verdict KEPT (product). The runs swung with the machine (pairs 1 and 4 read every worker 4–20 % cheaper on side B, as in the session's A/A), so read against the workers the change cannot reach in the same run: renderer −6.5, −3.9, −11.4, −4.4 % (median **−5.4 %, 4/4**), while those workers' own per-pair median was −9.6, +6.6, +6.3, −15.7 % (no consistent penalty). In the first sitting the same reading was −13.7, −15.4, −7.3, −9.7 % for the renderer with the others +8.8, +7.6, +3.0, +4.4 % in every pair.

So an upload straight from shared memory cost the rest of the engine about 6 % in Predator (most likely Chrome copying shared-memory uploads on other threads; not traced), and the copy removes it while the kernel keeps the renderer's gain. `wasm.pixiPack` stays on. W11's wiring (mesh batches in a mesh memory) uploads from shared views too: it needs the same copy, or a sitting that shows it does not matter.

records.title: The sprite collect in C for scenes without physics, W4b kernel
records.text: **kernel win (W4b, scenes without physics).** `wasm/preRenderCollect.c` is `collectVisibleEntities`' per-entity loop for sprites with no body (straight camera with or without the cull, and E-51's turned copy), writing the main collector as the JS does; a sprite with a layer mask is handed back to `collectRenderable` at its place in the walk. Bit for bit in seven cases (`preRenderCollectWasm.test.js`; an `or0` mutant without the NaN case fails all seven). Wired (`a3ca6cc7`, `44d3ce66`): with physics off, Transform, its pose and Collider move into the render-queue memory (E-112's `componentDataByte` path), and the shipped collect takes the kernel when every column is there and no body or Y-sort needs the JS loop. Kernel, `preRenderCollectWasmMicrobench` (250 000 sprites, the shipped collect with and without the kernel bound, Node 22, 5 alternating rounds): BunnyMark (skipCull, the sprite query's list) **350.6 → 489.4 ops/s, +39.6 %**; a culled camera over a world five times the view 232.4 → 298.9, **+28.6 %**; turned 212.8 → 252.0, **+18.4 %**; each 25/25. BunnyMark's owner pair follows in the scene batch.

records.title: The decal tile premultiply in C, W21c kernel and wiring
records.text: **kernel win.** `wasm/decalPremultiply.c` is `copyPremultiplyRgba` bit for bit: each colour byte `(c·a·257 + 32896) >> 16`, which is c at a = 255 and 0 at a = 0, so the JS's two fast cases are the general one and the SIMD loop has no branch; in 16-bit lanes `(t + (t >> 8)) >> 8` with t = c·a + 128, equal for all 65 536 (c, a) pairs (checked exhaustively). Wired in Pixi (`a49710ac`): each dirty tile is premultiplied from the decal memory (W26) into a scratch tile and copied into the tile's own array, which is uploaded (E-123: no upload from shared memory). Kernel, `decalPremultiplyWasmMicrobench` (decalStampStressScene's 40 tiles of 128 px after eight frames of its stamps, Node 22, 5 alternating rounds, the copy-out included): `copyPremultiplyRgba` **463.5 → 1 873.3 ops/s, +304.2 %** (SIMD, the shipped path), scalar 1 477.7 (+218.8 %), each 25/25.

records.title: Decal stamping wired on a decal memory, W26 kernel on the shipped path
records.text: **kernel win confirmed on the shipped path.** E-120's kernel (`wasm/decalStamp.c`, exact) is wired (`72853643`): the decal tiles move into a WebAssembly.Memory of their own at byte 0 (every worker views them as before), with a copy of each decal texture, the stamp records and the kernel's scratch after them, made once the textures are loaded (`installDecalMemory`). `stampParticleToTile` writes each stamp as a 64-byte record and `flushDecalStamps` stamps the frame's records in one call, then sets the dirty flags of the tiles they touched. `decalStampWired.test.js`: tiles and flags byte for byte against the JS over three frames (one past a flush's capacity, a texture outside the memory). Kernel, `decalStampWasmMicrobench` now through the worker's shipped path (768 stamps a frame, Node 22, 5 rounds): `Decal.stampToTileBuffers` **307.2 → 1 454.4 ops/s, +373.5 %** (25/25; E-120 read +377.9 % on its own wrapper); the scalar loop −10.6 %. The owner pair follows.

records.title: The mesh corner kernel with the UV generation, wired, W11 and E-118 kernels

records.title: The compound-solid raster in C without atan2, W1 kernel
records.text: **kernel win; a pseudo-angle replaces atan2.** An agent's `wasm/test/solidSegments.c` (`bc58a3ac`) ports `collectSolidSegments` with its raster. The polar bins are uniform in angle, so an end's bin comes from its octant and a table of tan(kπ/256), with no `atan2`; the cutoff and the wrap are cross/dot tests. Every variant stamps with the JS's own double `raySegT`, so a bin is identical or flipped: 0 flips on 8 stress-scene frames (98 304 bins) and a 257-light corpus; 468 flips only on 1 040 ends constructed on bin edges, within 1e-16 rad. `solidSegmentsWasmMicrobench` (compoundVisPoly `ringSegments=64` frames, Node 22, 5 rounds, 25/25 each): JS 273.3 frames/s; `f64` (fdlibm atan2) 320.1 (+17.1 %); `pseudo` 415.4 (+52.0 %); `fast` 484.2 (+77.1 %); `f64x2` 501.1 (+83.3 %); **`f32x4` 516.2 (+88.9 %)**. records.title: The sprite collect in C with bodies and the Y-sort foot line, W4b kernel (Phase 4)
records.text:
**Kernel win; Predator pair pending.** W4b's collect kernel now takes scenes with physics. Phase 4 put Transform's state block, RigidBody's, Collider's and both published pose buffers in Box2D's block, and workers bind Transform's heap pose on the block's buffer. So `collect_sprites` reads a body's latched pose and the one before it, and interpolates as `_displayPose` does.

The Y-sort foot line (`_storeEntitySortY`, `spriteSortFootY`, then `Math.round` with its halves and −0) is computed in C from the emit kernel's frame sizes. A sprite whose frame is not resolved yet goes to `collectRenderable`, as a masked one does. Each mode is a compiled copy of the walk, so the plain path carries no new test.

`preRenderCollectWasmMicrobench`, 250 000 sprites, 5 alternating rounds, every case won, checksums equal. Node; the machine was loaded by two agents' builds and tests.

| case | js ops/s | wasm ops/s | |
|---|---|---|---|
| predator (60 % bodies interpolated, Y-sort, mostly non-feet anchors, about a quarter queued) | 112.2 | 185.1 | **+65.0 %** |
| bunny | 351.3 | 494.6 | +40.8 % |
| cull | 230.4 | 297.5 | +29.1 % |
| turned | 211.4 | 252.2 | +19.3 % |

The three plain cases match this morning's sitting (+39.6 / 28.6 / 18.4 %), so the mode copies cost the plain walk nothing. A headless Predator smoke, one run each and not a pair, read `COLLECT_MS` 1.84 ms with the kernel off and 0.87 ms with it on.

Next: a Predator pair on one build, owner pre-render, `--query-a wasmOff=preRenderCollect`, on a quiet machine. Commits: 355839d3 (the kernel), a4e276ab (the bench case), b7de8bdb (the bodies' blocks in the block).

records.title: The bullet tick with its linecasts in C, W19 kernel (Node and Chrome)
records.text:
**Kernel win; wiring after E-129.** `wasm/bulletTick.c` puts `BulletPool.tick` and its `Ray.linecastDir` in one call per frame:
- the pool walk;
- the grid DDA of `_traverseGrid`;
- the filters of `_checkCellEntities`;
- the circle, box and single-polygon tests;
- the impact records;
- the active list;
- the slots that hit, which go back for the JS's `returnToPool` in walk order.

A cast that meets a compound polygon or a chain hands its bullet back before anything is written for it. `bulletTickWasm.test.js` checks the kernel bit for bit against the shipped tick: 4 000 bullets among 1 500 circles, boxes and rotated polygons, at three time steps and with every variant. A 0.02 % change to the box test fails it. The hand-back is tested too.

The pass covered:
- **flags:** two variants, both bit-identical: the box test's reciprocals once per ray (`hoist`), and no ray stamps (`nostamp`). A repeated test gives the same distance, which is never closer.
- **SIMD:** none. The walk is scalar per bullet, with a gather per candidate, so no lanes fill (the float32 pass's lesson).
- **float32:** not tried. Scalar f32 buys nothing over f64 on x86, and it would give up bit-identity.

`bulletTickWasmMicrobench`: bulletStressScene's world (4000 × 3000 px, cells of 128, 240 circles and boxes, four walls), a pool of 40 000 at 1500 px/s.

| | storm, 40 000 live | sparse, 4 000 live |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome 155, js | 262.7 ops/s | 2 074.6 ops/s |
| wasm | +61.0 % | +38.9 % |
| wasm_hoist | +62.1 % | +40.2 % |
| wasm_nostamp | +62.0 % | +40.2 % |
| **wasm_lean** (both) | **+63.5 %** | **+40.6 %** |
| Node, 5 alternating rounds | +73.7 to +80.2 % | +52.5 to +53.5 % |

Chrome ran every variant in one page over 7 alternating rounds, each 7/7 over the JS, checksums equal. The variants differ by about 2 %; `lean` was first in both cases and ships (9bc70782). The machine carried agents' builds and tests during both sittings.

An earlier smoke had inserted the walls into every cell their largest half extent covered; the bench now inserts each box by its own extents (81ae305d).

Next:
- E-129 widens the bullet pool.
- Then the wiring: the bullet columns in the bodies' part of Box2D's block, a dispatch in `BulletPool.tick` behind `wasm.bulletTick`, and a `bulletStressScene` pair on one build (owner particle).

records.title: Render-queue columns a cache line apart, E-113 kernel A/B
records.text:
**Kept (kernel).** Each render-queue column now starts at the next 64-byte boundary plus one line, measured from the queue's base, in `computeBufferSize` and `createViews`. That is the one layout every reader takes; the kernels take it through their tables. It adds about 1.6 KB per queue.

At a capacity that is a multiple of 1 024, every column of a row now falls in its own L1 set. `renderQueueColumnSkew.test.js` checks this; it fails on the old layout. At other capacities a set holds at most four columns.

`preRenderEmitWasmMicrobench`: the old layout from a worktree at HEAD against the new one, alternating processes, 5 rounds, checksums equal. Node; agents' builds and tests were on the machine.

| capacity | emit | old ops/s | new ops/s | | rounds won |

| 32 768 (aliased) | C | 900.8 | 2 162.0 | **+140 % (2.4×)** | 5/5 |
| 32 768 | JS | 863.0 | 964.2 | +11.7 % | 4/5 |
| 119 298 (Predator) | C | 2 144.9 | 2 175.5 | +1.4 % | 5/5 |

Still open:

records.title: The spawn sort by packed keys on the shipped method, E-125 kernel A/B
records.text:
**Kernel win; spawnStorm pair pending.** H-14 has been reapplied to the shipped `_processSpawnSoA`. Each spawn becomes a key, `entityIndex * span + position`, in a `Float64Array`. Its length is the batch capacity, a power of two from 256 that doubles, and it doubles as the span. The typed array's native numeric sort then gives the order the stable comparator sort over a permutation gave: by index, then by position. The position comes back exactly. `spawnSortParity.test.js` passes unchanged.

The 2026-10-14 kernel timed the sort strategies apart from the worker. The new `spawnSoAMicrobench` times the whole shipped method on a real logic worker: the sort, the duplicate drop, and the merges into the active list and the class lists. Each class owns a quarter of a 65 536-slot space, as an entity type owns its pool's range, and the batch draws 2 % repeats.

Writing the bench turned up two artifacts of a bare worker, both fixed before timing:
- **Merge scratch:** the merge allocated its scratch, because the worker's init sizes it and a bare worker never ran init.
- **Class layout:** random classes per index made one merge per spawn.

Old tree against new, alternating processes, 5 rounds, checksums equal. Node; agents' builds and tests were on the machine.

| case | old ops/s | new ops/s | | new won |

| storm: 1 024 spawns into 8 000 live | 5 427.3 | 7 491.6 | **+38.0 %** | 5/5 |
| batch: 256 into 20 000 | 7 235.4 | 7 823.4 | +8.1 % | 5/5 |
| trickle: 16 into 20 000 | 9 724.2 | 9 680.4 | −0.5 % | 2/5, a tie |

records.text:

Pre-render went from 4.364 to 3.757 ms: −13.3 % paired, worse 0/4. Against the other workers it reads −17.3 % (lower 4/4). Load keys are within 1 %: bodies 17 549 → 17 569, visible +0.9 %, queue +0.8 %.

records.title: The split upload for plain sprites, BunnyMarkStressC and Predator pairs, E-82b
records.text:
**kept (product).** The split upload for sprites without pose interpolation (`wasm.gpuPackSplit`, default on), built as the 2026-10-24 design note asked: in the packer.

How it works:
- `gpuPack.wasm` gains `pack_sprites_split` and its scatter (b0ec6ca8). They write each plain sprite's pose (x, y, rotC, rotS: 16 bytes) and, when asked, its statics (44 bytes, E-82's static order). The values are bit for bit those of the 15-float row: `gpuPackSplit.test.js`, through the gather and the scatter.
- Pre-render writes the main sprites into its GPU queue as the two streams (`GPU_FLAG_SPLIT`, the statics' generation in the header). It writes the statics only into a GPU queue buffer that lacks the queue's `staticGen` for the same rows.
- The glow split's list (the rows that are not glows, in order) follows from the types and so from the generation. A painter-sorted frame always writes both streams.
- Pixi's entity batch is E-82's two-stream batch with a 16-byte pose, the previous xy read from the current one (the pose shader's mix at alpha 1). It copies and uploads the statics only when the generation or the row count moves (a37217a6).
- A frame whose statics change uploads the same 60 bytes a sprite as before. A nearest atlas, whose poses snap, keeps 15-float rows.

Measuring tool: `?bunnies=` on BunnyMarkStressCScene (f7d7ae5d). At 100 000 bunnies the split left Pixi under the floor (headless 1.93 → 0.80 ms).

**Owner pair.** BunnyMarkStressC at 250 000 bunnies (still camera, no Y-sort), one build (a37217a6 as f57b390f), side A `wasmOff=gpuPackSplit`, headed, source, detailed stats off, exact windows, 4 pairs, `--owner renderer`:
- renderer 4.953 → 1.701 ms, **−65.6 %**, worse 0/4, cv 2/2 %;
- pre-render 9.212 → 7.006 ms, **−23.8 %**, worse 0/4 (16 bytes written a sprite on a persist frame instead of 60);
- logic 2.501 → 2.533 (under the floor); 250 000 rows on both sides.

**Predator guard.** Its sprites take Pixi's SoA path into the split batch, painter-sorted, so their statics move every frame. Renderer, one build, 4 pairs: NEUTRAL. Renderer 3.517 → 3.480 ms (−3.1 % paired, 2/4 worse, +1.1 % against the others); no worker 3 % worse in 3 of 4; load within 0.6 %.

Tests:
- `instancedSpriteSplit.test.js` (the batch on every path, the static uploads);
- `gpuPackSplitWired.test.js` (pre-render's GPU queue on the real worker: the streams equal the rows of the switch-off run, which buffer rewrites its statics when, a painter-sorted frame every time);
- `gpuPackSplitPixi.test.js` (Pixi's commit of split and row frames, and a plain batch never reading a split frame as rows).

Screenshots of BunnyMark (on and off), Predator, and painterMove on WebGPU draw as before.

Left:
- the same split for a nearest atlas (the pose with the pixel snap);
- pose interpolation on the packed path (pre-render writing the previous xy, 24 bytes);
- packed static formats (E-82's half floats).
